The Story of Dharmaghosh Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who teaches the true dharma and is therefore the lord of the entire world, and I write the story of Shri Dharmaghosh Muni.

After a month-long fast, the embodiment of dharma, Shri Dharmaghosh Muni, one day broke his fast in a neighbourhood of Champapuri and was returning toward the meditation grove. Having lost his way, he had to walk a long distance on fresh green grass. The exertion of walking made him tired and thirsty. He came and sat under a shady tree on the bank of the Ganga.

Seeing the monk somewhat distressed by thirst, Goddess Ganga came to him with a pot full of pure, cool water. She said, "Yogiraj, I have brought cold water for you. Please drink and quench your thirst." The monk replied, "Devi, you have done your duty — this is fitting for you. But food and water given by gods is not acceptable to monks."

Hearing this, the goddess was greatly surprised. She immediately went to the Videha region to learn the reason. There she bowed to the omniscient Lord and asked, "Bhagavan, I went to give water to a thirsty monk, but he did not drink the water from my hand. What is the reason?" The Lord replied, "Devi, monks cannot accept food or water given by gods."

Hearing the Lord's answer, the goddess was at a loss. Then she began to shower fragrant, cool water all around the monk for his comfort. Through this, the monk attained peace. Afterward, through the meditation called Shukla-dhyana, he destroyed his destructive karmas. Finally, having set only worthy souls on the path of self-welfare, he attained nirvana.

May those Monk Dharmaghosh, who possess the eye of omniscience to see the subtlest states of things, who engage worthy souls on the path of welfare, who know the world and beyond, who are worshipped by the gods, and who are the sun that dispels the dense darkness of delusion and false faith for worthy souls — may they make you and me happy.

This story teaches the strict discipline of monastic life. Monks must not accept food or water from gods, for their sustenance must come only from the charitable giving of human householders. This rule ensures that monks remain humble and dependent on the merit of human beings, not on supernatural beings. Goddess Ganga herself could not break this rule, and the monk's adherence to it shows the depth of his commitment to the monastic code. The wise should respect and follow the rules of their spiritual tradition with sincerity.
